name: めんきや 京都壬生本店 (Menkiya Kyoto Mibu Honten)

claims.text: Wheat noodles, a wheat-based soy-sauce tare, and shared cooking equipment make this unsafe for celiac diners; no gluten-free handling is indicated.
The signature bowl is a back-fat shoyu (soy-sauce) ramen; the tare is virtually certainly standard wheat-containing shoyu.
Broth is pork-bone and back fat with pork chashu; no vegan or vegetarian option is offered, so all bowls share an animal-based base.

name: 麺匠 一粒万倍 寺町店 (Mensho Ichiryu Manbai Teramachi)

claims.text: Wheat noodles are the core product and the thick tsukemen noodles contain bran (ふすま); shared noodle-cooking water and a wheat-based soy tare make this a high-gluten environment.
The 醤油 (soy) ramen uses a soy-based tare, which in standard Japanese shoyu contains wheat. No wheat-free tare is mentioned.
Every broth is animal-based (duck/chicken clear soup or pork-bone-and-fish tsukemen) and toppings include pork and chicken chashu; no plant-based preparation exists.
An English menu is available and the shop is used to international customers, which can make it easier to ask questions about ingredients.

name: 麺匠 たか松 本店 (Mensho Takamatsu Honten)

claims.text: Wheat noodles and a wheat-shoyu-based tare are central to every bowl; there is no separate gluten-free preparation and cross-contact with wheat is unavoidable in a small tsukemen kitchen.
The chicken-seafood dipping broth is built on a soy-based tare, which in standard Japanese ramen/tsukemen contains wheat unless stated otherwise; no wheat-free shoyu is indicated.
All bowls use an animal (chicken plus katsuo/saba/scallop) broth; no plant-based stock or vegan option is offered, so there is nothing safe for a strict vegan.

name: メントメシ ザコヤ (Mentomeshi Zakoya)

claims.text: House-made wheat ramen noodles are the base of the dish; no gluten-free option was found.
A soy-sauce seasoned seafood bowl and shoyu ramen are on the menu; the tare is presumed conventional wheat-based soy sauce. No wheat-free tare is indicated.
Entirely seafood-based kitchen with dashi from sea bream, scallop, ribbonfish and dried sardines plus fish toppings and a seasoned egg, so any dish involves fish and likely egg.
All dishes are meat-free (no pork or chicken), built entirely on fish and seafood.

name: 麺屋 栩羚廚 壬生本店 (Menya Craze Mibu Honten)

claims.text: Bowls use wheat ramen noodles (from the Teigaku/棣鄂 maker) cooked in shared boiling water, and the karaage side is flour-dredged and deep-fried; no gluten-free handling is indicated.
The core 濃厚豚骨醤油 and the tare layered over the 極濃豚骨 are soy-sauce based, which in Japan is almost always brewed with wheat.
Every bowl is built on a pork-bone broth with animal toppings (chashu, egg); there is no separate vegan prep area or plant-based option.

name: 麺屋 極鶏 一乗寺本店 (Menya Gokkei Ichijoji Honten)

claims.text: Single-concept ramen shop: wheat noodles and a soy-sauce-seasoned chicken broth are central to every bowl, with no gluten-free option or separate preparation. Not suitable for strict gluten avoidance.
The broth is seasoned with a soy-sauce-based tare; Japanese soy sauce almost always contains wheat, so the soup itself is not gluten-free.
All bowls are built on chicken broth and chicken toppings; there is no plant-based broth, so vegan diners cannot be served.
Wheat ramen noodles, a soy-sauce-based tare, and shared broth/cooking water make cross-contamination with gluten effectively unavoidable for a celiac diner.
The signature bowl is a 濃厚豚骨醤油 (pork-bone soy-sauce) ramen; the tare is soy-sauce based, which in standard ramen contains wheat.
All broths and dishes are animal-based (pork bone and chicken stock with chashu, egg, and karaage); no vegan preparation or separation is described.
The dish itself contains multiple wheat sources — wheat ramen noodles plus a fresh fu (wheat gluten) topping — so cross-contamination is moot; the ramen is inherently not gluten-free.
The broth is a white-miso tare; Kyoto white miso commonly contains wheat or barley, and the dashi is bonito/kombu or shellfish based. No wheat-free tare is indicated.
Broth is built on bonito/kombu or shellfish dashi and bowls include smoked chashu pork and egg; plant toppings (yuba, fu) sit in an animal-based soup, so a vegan-safe bowl is not offered.
